The Great Sandy Desert. A large hot desert occupying roughly seventy-five thousand square miles of northwestern Australia, spanning parts of Western Australia and the Northern Territory. An interior arid plateau characterized by extensive sand dunes, minimal water sources, and sparse vegetation, it has been home to Aboriginal peoples whose cultural knowledge sustained settlement for tens of thousands of years.

The second-largest desert in Australia, it is characterized by longitudinal, or linear, sand dunes that can stretch for tens of miles in parallel ridges. Temperatures in summer regularly exceed forty-five degrees Celsius, or one hundred and thirteen degrees Fahrenheit. Winter nights can drop near freezing. Rainfall is erratic and minimal, typically less than eight inches annually.

Aboriginal peoples have inhabited the region for at least forty thousand years, using sophisticated knowledge of hidden water sources and seasonal resource availability. The desert contains sparse vegetation adapted to aridity: mulga, spinifex grass, and scattered shrubs. Kangaroos, dingoes, and reptiles are the primary fauna.

European exploration of the interior was difficult and dangerous. The desert's vastness made early mapping incomplete, and many explorers perished. Traditional Aboriginal land boundaries cross the desert. Various language groups—Martu, Walmajarri, Pitjantjatjara—maintain cultural and spiritual connections to the region.

Modern mining, particularly of iron ore and rare earth elements, has increased economic and environmental pressure on the desert. The Great Sandy Desert occupies northwestern Australia's interior, serving as ancestral territory for Aboriginal custodians with deep ecological knowledge. Songlines and dreaming stories map the desert, connecting it to indigenous Australian culture in ways that predate written history by tens of thousands of years.
